body.en: Henri Fayol (1841–1925), the father of general management, gave 14 *principles*: division of work; authority and responsibility (in balance); discipline; unity of command (one boss for each employee); unity of direction (one head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective); subordination of individual interest to general interest; remuneration of employees (fair pay); centralisation and decentralisation (a proper balance); scalar chain (a formal line of authority, with a gang plank for quick communication between equals); order (a place for everything and everyone); equity (fairness and kindness); stability of tenure; initiative; and esprit de corps (team spirit).

points.en: Division of work; authority and responsibility
Unity of command and unity of direction
Order, equity, stability, initiative, esprit de corps

body.en: *Fayol* looked at management from the top (general principles for managers at all levels, from his experience as a manager); Taylor looked from the shop floor (increasing the productivity of workers by scientific study, from his experience as an engineer). Fayol stressed unity of command; Taylor's functional foremanship gave a worker eight bosses, which violates it. Fayol's principles apply universally; Taylor's techniques apply mainly to production. Together they replaced rule-of-thumb management with systematic thinking.

points.en: Functional foremanship vs unity of command
Both: systematic, not rule of thumb

say.en: Standard output is 10 units a day; rates are 50 rupees a unit at or above standard and 40 rupees below. A makes 12 units, B makes 9. Find their wages and the difference.
A reaches the standard: 12 times 50 rupees equals 600 rupees.
B is below the standard: 9 times 40 rupees equals 360 rupees.
Difference equals 240 rupees for just 3 more units.
The large gap motivates workers to reach the standard.
So the answer is A 600, rupees B 360 rupees; difference 240 rupees.
